blocks.title: Repairs, new zones, **upkeep.**
body: Our irrigation work comes in three kinds: fixing what is broken, adding coverage where the lawn needs it, and keeping a system running well through the season. A zone that will not come on, a head soaking the street, a corner of the lawn that is always brown: that is the call.
We keep it simple. Rob comes out, looks at the system with you, tells you plainly what he sees and quotes what it needs. The estimate is free.

items.title: A zone that will not run
items.body: One part of the lawn stays dry while the rest comes on. Worth a look before that side of the yard browns out in July.

items.title: Water on the concrete
items.body: Heads that spray the drive, the walk or the street waste water and leave the grass short of it. They need to be set to hit the lawn.

items.title: Dry arcs and brown corners
items.body: Uneven coverage shows up as brown arcs between heads or a corner that never greens up. MSU Extension's can test, below, shows where the water is not landing.

items.title: Runoff and soggy spots
items.body: MSU says a system should never put water down faster than the soil can take it in. On clay or a slope, shorter cycles run more than once give the water time to soak in instead of running off.

blocks.title: How much water **a Michigan lawn** needs.
blocks.intro: Michigan State University Extension's guidance, in short. A system that runs right gets the lawn close to these numbers.

items.title: About an inch a week
items.body: A lawn usually needs about 1 inch of water a week, MSU says, and rain counts toward it. Across a season MSU's range is 0.5 to 1.5 inches, more in heat, full sun and wind. A rain gauge tells you what already fell.

items.title: Split it up
items.body: MSU research found several light waterings work better than one heavy soak a week. On sandy soil that may mean every other day, and on heavier soil every third day.

items.title: Daylight or late night
items.body: MSU calls early evening one of the worst times to water, because the grass stays wet overnight and disease can follow. Daylight works, and when there are restrictions, midnight to 6 a.m. is acceptable.

items.title: Measure what it puts down
items.body: Set a few rain gauges or tuna cans around the lawn, run the system for an hour and check what each one caught. MSU says that tells you how long a zone needs, and where coverage is uneven.

items.title: Shut it off in the rain
items.body: MSU recommends a rain shut off device on a system that runs on a clock, and turning the clock off through a rainy stretch, so the lawn is not watered on top of the weather.

items.title: Before a hard freeze
items.body: MSU's fall checklist includes blowing out or winterizing the irrigation system before a hard freeze. Ask Rob about fall service when you book.

blocks.title: Sprinklers and **a weekly cut.**
body: Water and mowing work together. MSU Extension notes that cool season lawns go dormant in a long hot, dry spell, and that irrigation can keep them green through the summer. A higher cut helps too: MSU says taller grass keeps a bigger root system and holds up better in the heat. Pair a working system with [weekly mowing](/lawn-mowing/) and the stripes still show in August.

Letting the lawn go brown in July is a fair choice as well. MSU says a dormant lawn is not dead, since the crown of the plant stays alive waiting for water. Its one warning: if you have been watering, taper off gradually rather than shutting the system off all at once in the heat.

faq.q: Do you repair sprinkler systems in Grand Blanc?

faq.q: How much should I water my lawn in Michigan?
faq.a: About 1 inch a week, counting rain, according to MSU Extension, with a range of 0.5 to 1.5 inches depending on heat, sun and wind. Split it into several waterings rather than one long soak. A rain gauge in the yard tells you how much the weather already covered.

faq.q: What time of day should my sprinklers run?
faq.a: During the day or in the middle of the night. MSU Extension says early evening is one of the worst times, because the grass stays wet overnight and some lawn diseases become active. When watering is restricted, MSU says midnight to 6 a.m. is acceptable.

faq.q: How do I know how long to run each zone?
faq.a: Measure it. MSU Extension suggests setting rain gauges or tuna cans around the lawn, running the system for an hour and checking how much each one caught. That shows how long it takes to put down what the lawn needs, and where the coverage is uneven.

faq.q: Do I need to winterize my sprinkler system in Michigan?
faq.a: MSU Extension's fall checklist says to blow out or winterize the irrigation system before a hard freeze. Ask Rob about fall service when you call, and he can tell you what fits your system.

faq.q: Can you add a zone to my sprinkler system?
faq.a: Yes. New lines and zones are part of our irrigation work, for a corner that never gets water or a part of the yard the system never reached. Rob will look at the system, see what it can take and quote it.

faq.q: How much does sprinkler repair cost?
faq.a: It depends on what is wrong and how much of the system is involved. Rob comes out, looks at it and quotes you a price before any work starts. The estimate is free.
